Lost in the clouds: Your private data has been indexed by Google

I am not really surprised this happened. The only thing I can say is that nobody forces you to use these services, and you clicked the "I Agree" button to these terms and conditions. If you want your data private, store it on a USB thumb drive and store it in your desk drawer, I doubt Google will be indexing those files any time soon.

Did you even read the article?

It wasn't about corporate clouds sharing data with the Internet/NSA - it was about Google inadvertently indexing private data when people have shared it to the world in the form of a publicly accessible website.
always remember, if you're getting something for free, you're not the consumer, you're the product

http://www.csoonline.com seems to be the Jezebel version of a computer security website.

"Hey, did you know that uploading your private data to a giant world-wide computer network run by scumbag corporations who own your government makes that data no longer private?"

Shocking!

Google tries to index just about everything that they can to make the search engine better, should they adjust their index engine so it doesn't do FTP? I don't think they would do that. The next best thing is to somehow educate the average consumers that their routers aren't dumb anymore, and they should really read the manual before they start change settings they don't understand.

The article was phrased a bit oddly - they seemed to try to give the impression that private Google Drive or Dropbox files were publicly accessible, or that some TOS trickery was going on.

Basically, the situation the article is actually describing is when people buy a personal cloud (preconfigured NAS) and don't know what they're doing - so they hook it into the big Word Wide Web and set it up as a public website, making all their files publicly accessible. Google does what it's supposed to, and indexes it.

Basically, this article is nothing new - put a password on things that store sensitive data, and you'll be A-OK. Don't put a password, and you're 1 mistake away from having everybody and their grandma be able to hack you.

Wrong. Google, Microsoft, and Apple allow ALL their users' data to be stored in NSA datacenters where it is cataloged and shared with other companies regardless of whether the user specifies that data is public or private.

I am very aware of the issues with cloud services - but (if you'll actually read the article), you'll see that that's not what they're referring to.

Yes, the title heavily implied that the article was about Google/Apple sharing private cloud data with the NSA, but it was misleading - nothing more than "clickbait" trying to make an article which simply reminds people to put a password on their NASes look like an article about NSA surveillance and corporate corruption.

This article was specifically talking about "Googledorks" - people who have accidentally set their own computers/NASes up as public websites, which then get indexed (inadvertently on both parties' parts, but preventably on the user's part) and added to Google's list of public websites.

Useful tips for parents who have no clue what video games are about. There's a lot more shit today that parents have to protect their kids from. Back in the day you just hooked up the NES and the biggest problem was how many times you had to blow on the cartridge. It seems strange to me so many parents still know so little about the subject. I grew up with video games and I'm beyond old enough to be a parent myself. Granted I grew up in that NES era and things were different- but I still play a lot of games and I keep up to speed with trends. I feel like if I did have children I'd be pretty well informed about the dangers kids could face. As a father of a 7 year old gamer I really appreciate his handling of this. He is spot on when it comes to general advice for parents who are not gamers. Brilliant.

Personally my daughter plays all kinds of games. She's beaten several Halos and I even let her play Borderlands with me. We play Diablo 3 together and she's got a 50+ Paragon in Hardcore.

We talk about what is and isn't ok. Profanity. Vulgarity. What fantasy is compared to reality. We talk about why she can play games like Borderlands WITH me, but not on her own, and why her friends probably can't play it at all.

Video games have greatly helped her with school. She was having some difficulty with reading, less difficulty and more a motivation issue, she hated it and I couldn't get her excited about reading. So we started playing Final Fantasy 9 together. I made her read, we would share the lines, I'd read Zidane's lines and she would read Dagger's. It hooked her and now she's reading above her level (and really into Final Fantasy).

Good job Gabe, thanks for dispelling the horrible game stereotypes in a way that is educational and useful for parents.
